summary: Describes the frame format for sending IPv6 packets over IEEE 1394 networks, and how to form link-local and stateless autoconfigured IPv6 addresses on them.

plainLanguage.summary: It explains how to send Internet packages through a FireWire cable and how devices pick their own addresses.

questions: how does ipv6 work over ieee 1394
what is the ipv6 ether type for 1394
what is the default mtu for ipv6 over firewire
how is the ipv6 interface identifier formed on ieee 1394
subtitle: How IPv6 packets ride on IEEE 1394 (FireWire-style) buses: framing, addresses, neighbor lookup and multicast.

tldr.problem: IPv6 needs a defined way to run over each kind of link. IEEE 1394 already had a method for carrying IPv4 and ARP, but nothing said how to carry IPv6 or build IPv6 addresses on it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reuses the IPv4-over-1394 encapsulation and fragmentation, sets the IPv6 ether_type to 0x86dd, builds interface identifiers from the interface's EUI-64, and defines the 1394 form of the Neighbor Discovery link-layer address option and rules for multicast.
tldr.outcome: IPv6 nodes on a 1394 bus can form link-local and autoconfigured addresses, find each other and send multicast. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that has since been updated by RFC 8064.

today: RFC 3146 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8064. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IEEE Std 1394-1995 defines a High Performance Serial Bus. The IETF IP1394 Working Group had already standardized how to carry IPv4 datagrams and ARP packets over an IEEE 1394 subnetwork, in RFC 2734.

This RFC does the same job for IPv6. It describes the frame format for IPv6 packets, the way to form IPv6 link-local addresses and statelessly autoconfigured addresses, and the content of the Source/Target Link-layer Address option used in Neighbor Discovery when messages travel over 1394.

Much of the work is done by reference: wherever the IPv4 document already solves a problem, this RFC says to do the same thing.
sections.plainLanguage: FireWire already knew how to carry the old kind of Internet addresses. This document teaches it to carry the new, longer kind too.

sections.title: Node Requirements and Configuration ROM
sections.content:
An IPv6-capable node MUST meet four minimum requirements. It MUST implement configuration ROM in the general format of ISO/IEC 13213:1994, with the bus information block from IEEE Std 1394a-2000 and a unit directory defined by this document. Its max_rec field MUST be at least 8, meaning it can accept block write requests and asynchronous stream packets with a 512-octet payload, and can send a block response with a 512-octet payload. It MUST be isochronous resource manager capable. It MUST support both reception and transmission of asynchronous streams.

The unit directory follows the IPv4-over-1394 format with two changes. The Unit_SW_Version value is 0x000002, and its textual descriptor MUST be IPv6. A dual-stack node (IPv4 and IPv6) has two unit directories, one for each protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a device can join in, it has to carry a name tag that says it speaks IPv6 and promise it can handle packages of a certain size.

sections.title: Encapsulation, Fragmentation and MTU
sections.content:
Encapsulation and fragmentation MUST be exactly as in section 4 of RFC 2734. Because an ether_type field tells IPv4 and IPv6 apart, and because MCAP (multicast channel allocation protocol) is shared by both, the version field in the GASP (global asynchronous stream packet) header of IPv6 datagrams has the same value as for IPv4, which is one. The ether_type value for IPv6 is 0x86dd.

The default MTU for IPv6 packets on an IEEE 1394 network is 1500 octets. It can be lowered by a Router Advertisement carrying an MTU option with a smaller value, or by manual configuration of each node. If a Router Advertisement names an MTU larger than 1500, or larger than a manually configured value, the option may be logged to system management but MUST otherwise be ignored. A way to extend the MTU between two particular nodes is left for further study.
sections.plainLanguage: Packages on the cable are normally no bigger than 1500 bytes. A router can ask for smaller ones, but it can never talk a device into bigger ones.

sections.title: Interface Identifiers and Link-Local Addresses
sections.content:
The Interface Identifier for an IEEE 1394 interface comes from the interface's built-in EUI-64 identifier, with the Universal/Local (U/L) bit complemented. The U/L bit is the next-to-lowest order bit of the first octet. A universally administered EUI-64 has a 0 there, while a globally unique IPv6 Interface Identifier has a 1, so the flip will generally turn a 0 into a 1.

An IPv6 address prefix used for stateless autoconfiguration of an IEEE 1394 interface MUST be 64 bits long.

The link-local address is the prefix FE80::/64 followed by the Interface Identifier: 10 bits of 1111111010, 54 bits of zeros and the 64-bit identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Every FireWire gadget has a serial number burned in. The IPv6 address is made from that number, with one small switch flipped, so no two gadgets end up with the same address.

sections.title: Finding Neighbors: Unicast Address Mapping
sections.content:
Mapping an IPv6 unicast address to a 1394 link-layer address uses Neighbor Discovery. The 1394 node_ID is not placed in the Link-layer Address option, because it is not constant across a 1394 bridge. Instead, the recipient SHOULD combine the source_ID (from the asynchronous packet header or the GASP header) with the content of the Source link-layer address. An implementation MAY use another method to learn the sender's node_ID, such as a table mapping node_unique_ID to node_ID; how to build that table is out of scope.

The recipient of a Neighbor Discovery packet MUST ignore it unless the most significant ten bits of the source_ID equal either 0x3FF or the most significant ten bits of the recipient's NODE_IDS register.

The option has Length 3 (units of 8 octets) and carries the node's unique ID, max_rec, spd (the lesser of link speed and PHY speed) and a 48-bit unicast_FIFO offset. The offset MUST NOT change except through a power reset. Reserved bits are zero when sent and ignored on receipt. Because node_ID can change on a 1394 bus reset, the mapping cache SHOULD be cleared on bus reset.
sections.plainLanguage: To send a package to a neighbor, you need to know which plug on the bus it is in. The neighbor writes down its serial number and abilities on a card, and everyone reads that card.

sections.title: IPv6 Multicast
sections.content:
By default, all best-effort IPv6 multicast MUST use asynchronous stream packets on the channel number found in the channel field of the BROADCAST_CHANNEL register. This is mandatory for datagrams sent to the all-nodes, all-routers and solicited-node multicast addresses.

Other multicast groups may use a different channel if one is allocated and advertised first, using MCAP as described in RFC 2734. A node that wants to receive such groups MUST first confirm through MCAP that a channel mapping exists. MCAP is optional for send-only nodes, which MAY send any multicast data on the default broadcast channel. To send on another channel, a node MUST first confirm by MCAP whether a channel is already allocated. Implementors are encouraged to use MCAP for high-rate multicast streams. The MCAP type value for an IPv6 group address descriptor is 2.
sections.plainLanguage: Shouting to everyone goes on one shared loudspeaker channel. If a group wants its own private channel, it has to announce it first so listeners can tune in.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA assigned 0x000002 as the Unit_SW_Version for IPv6 over IEEE 1394 from the CSR Protocol Identifiers name space.

The RFC also asks IANA to maintain the 8-bit MCAP group address descriptor type name space defined by RFC 2734. The initial assignments are 0 reserved, 1 IPv4 Multicast Address, 2 IPv6 Multicast Address and 255 reserved. Values 3 to 254 can be assigned through Standards Action.
sections.plainLanguage: Some numbers must be written in an official list so nobody uses them for something else. This document adds the IPv6 entries to that list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that IPv6 over IEEE 1394 does not introduce any additional security considerations beyond those of RFC 2734. The concerns described in the security section of that document apply here as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Running IPv6 on FireWire adds no new dangers beyond the ones the older FireWire document already described.

viz.caption: SOURCE/TARGET LINK-LAYER ADDRESS OPTION FOR IEEE 1394 (RFC 3146)

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: 1 for Source Link-layer address, 2 for Target Link-layer address.

fields.name: node_unique_ID
fields.desc: EUI-64 identifier; MUST equal the value in the node's configuration ROM.

fields.name: max_rec
fields.desc: MUST equal max_rec in the node's configuration ROM.

fields.name: spd
fields.desc: The lesser of the link speed and the PHY speed.

fields.name: unicast_FIFO
fields.desc: 48-bit offset of the FIFO for receiving IPv6 datagrams.

fields.name: reserved
fields.desc: All zeros from the sender, ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: Prefix 1111111010
fields.desc: The FE80::/64 prefix begins with these 10 bits.

fields.name: Interface Identifier
fields.desc: Built from the EUI-64 with the U/L bit complemented.
